items.title: Jocasta
items.text:
Jocasta keeps an inventory of the devices on your network. It logs every change. It is one binary, with a web UI, a JSON API and an MCP server.

Pre-1.0

A release can change the config format, the database schema or the API with no upgrade path. Pin a version. Before you move to a new version, read the upgrade notes. To read the docs for your release, select it in the version menu at the top.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. Jocasta sweeps the networks you list, or the network of the host, every 5 minutes.
  2. It records each device under its hardware address, because an IP address is only a lease.
  3. It logs what changed.

To see other VLANs, add your router. To see traffic, add flow exports. To see lookups, add your DNS resolver.

items.title: How a device gets its type
items.text:
After each scan, Jocasta guesses the type of each device from these facts:

  • the vendor of its hardware address
  • its name
  • its open TCP ports
  • the DNS-SD services it advertises, and the model of a Google Cast device
  • whether it made up its hardware address
  • the name of its network, such as IoT
  • whether it has the .1 address of its subnet

items.title: Rules
items.text:
Each rule names a type and the facts it needs. For example, vendor Brother means a printer, and port 8123 means a Home Assistant hub. Of the rules that match, the rule with the most facts wins. If two rules have the same number of facts, the rule listed first wins.

The device page shows the guess as auto, with a confidence:

  • High: the rule needs two or more facts, or two rules agree.
  • Low: the guess comes from one weak fact, such as the network's name, and nothing else.
  • Medium: all other cases.

If a later scan changes the guess, the change log records Type changed.

items.title: Set the type yourself
items.text:
1. Open the device and select Edit details.
  2. Select a type.
  3. Select Save.

Scans never change a type that you set. The device page still shows the guess. To use the guess again, select Auto.

items.text: The explain_device tool of the MCP server returns the facts, the rule that won, and every other rule that matched.

items.title: CLI
items.text:
jocasta <command> [flags]

  serve              Start the web server and the sweep poller.  (default)
  scan <cidr>        Sweep a prefix once and print the result.
  ports [target]     Probe TCP ports on an address, a prefix, or the inventory.
  plugin run <name>  Read one configured source and print what it claims.
  version            Print build information.

  -c, --config       Path to the config file (default "jocasta.yaml")
      --log-level    debug | info | warn | error
      --log-format   text | json

To see the flags of a command, run it with --help.

items.title: serve
items.text:
jocasta serve                 # host and port from config
jocasta serve -p 9000         # override the port

Starts the HTTP server. It also starts these tasks:

  • If scan.devices.enabled is set, a poller sweeps every network in networks at each scan.devices.interval.
  • If scan.ports.enabled is set, a second poller port-scans every address that the inventory has on your networks, at each scan.ports.interval. It also port-scans each new device when a sweep or a router read finds it.
  • At each scan.devices.interval, Jocasta reads each enabled routeros and openwrt instance for what is connected to it.
  • Each enabled netflow instance starts a listener for the flow exports of its router.
  • Each hour, a prune deletes records that are older than their retention window. It also deletes devices that you never edited and that no scan saw within retention.devices.

items.title: scan
items.text:
Runs one sweep and prints a table, or JSON with --json. With --save, it also records the sweep in the inventory. The source name comes from --source. If that is not set, it comes from scan.source, and then from the name of this host.

$ jocasta scan 192.0.2.0/24
IP           MAC                VENDOR   HOSTNAME              RTT     DETAILS
192.0.2.1    00:00:5e:00:53:01  -        gateway.example      1.2ms
192.0.2.10   00:00:5e:00:53:02  -        nas.example          0.8ms
192.0.2.20   00:00:5e:00:53:04  -        -                    3.1ms   self (eth0)

$ jocasta scan 192.0.2.0/24 --save --rate 500 --no-resolve-names

The sweep uses a raw ICMP socket if it can. If not, it uses an unprivileged datagram socket. So it runs without root. If a host has no reverse DNS name, the sweep asks for its name over mDNS, then NetBIOS, then DNS-SD, then SSDP. It stops when one of them gives a name. To turn each one off, use --no-resolve-mdns, --no-resolve-netbios, --no-resolve-dnssd or --no-resolve-ssdp. With --json, each host also lists the services that it advertises over DNS-SD.

items.title: ports
items.text:
Probes TCP ports with a plain connect(). So it needs no privileges and cannot change the target.

With no argument, it scans every current address that the inventory has on your networks. Your networks are those in networks and the segments that a router serves. It does not scan a neighbour outside them, such as the gateway of your ISP. It also scans each address on these TCP ports:

  • the ports on which its device advertises a service
  • the ports recorded as open on that device

To scan only one address or prefix, give it as the argument.

--ports takes a list such as 22,80,443,8000-8100. By default, it scans a preset of about a hundred ports that homelabs often use. --concurrency sets the maximum number of open connections at one time (64 by default). --save records the results on the matching devices.

$ jocasta ports 192.0.2.10
ADDRESS      PORT   SERVICE
192.0.2.10   22     ssh
192.0.2.10   443    https

$ jocasta ports --save                      # every known address, recorded
$ jocasta ports 192.0.2.0/24 --ports 1-1024 --json

items.title: plugin run
items.text:
Reads one configured source without starting the server. Use it to test a credential or a firewall rule against the real router. It reads the instance even when the config disables it.

$ jocasta plugin run gateway
NETWORK           VLAN  NAME
192.0.2.0/24      -     Trusted
198.51.100.0/24   20    IoT

ADDRESS          MAC                VENDOR  HOSTNAME    STANDING     PRESENT
192.0.2.1        00:00:5e:00:53:01  -       gateway     DHCP_STATIC  true
198.51.100.10    00:00:5e:00:53:09  -       thermostat  DHCP_LEASE   true

$ jocasta plugin run gateway --json --save

After the devices, it prints the topology of the source:

  • its ports, and the VLANs on each port
  • the hardware addresses that it learned on each port
  • its neighbours

A topology_only instance prints only the topology. --save records both.

items.title: Devices
items.text:
Jocasta identifies a device by its hardware (MAC) address. An IP address is only a lease. So your label and notes stay with the device when its IP address changes.

A sweep reads hardware addresses only on its own segment. Jocasta knows a device on another segment by its IP address until a router reports its hardware address. The device page shows which: by hardware address or by IP address. If a record for that hardware address already exists, Jocasta merges the two and keeps your labels.

Phones, tablets and laptops make up a new hardware address for each Wi-Fi network. Such an address names no vendor, and each new address is a new device. Jocasta deletes a device 90 days after a scan last saw it, unless you gave it a label, group, type or notes, or ignored or watched it.

If a device stops answering on an address, Jocasta removes that address after the device answers on a different address in the same network for 6 hours.

items.title: Networks
items.text: A network is an IP prefix, such as 192.0.2.0/24. Jocasta sweeps the prefixes under networks. If you list none, it sweeps the network of the host. A router plugin adds the segments that the router serves, with their names and VLAN tags.

items.title: Scans
items.text:
A scan is one recorded reading:

  • Sweep. An ICMP echo to every address in networks, then a name lookup for each address that answers. Every 5 minutes.
  • Port scan. A TCP connection to a list of ports on every known address. Off until you set scan.ports.enabled: true, then every 6 hours. Jocasta also scans a new device when a sweep or a router read finds it.
  • Plugin read. A router's ARP and DHCP tables, read with each sweep. A DNS resolver's query log, read every minute.

The Scans page lists them. To start a scan yourself, use jocasta scan, jocasta ports or jocasta plugin run.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
Each scan records its facts under a source. The sweep's source is sweep:<host>. A plugin's source is its instance name, such as gateway. The device page lists the name that each source gives the device.

If two sources give different names, the source with the higher standing wins. For example, a static DHCP lease wins over a name that the device announces. See How names are chosen.

items.title: Presence
items.text:
A device is seen recently if a scan saw it in the last 15 minutes. If not, it is quiet. Both states come from past scans. A page that you open does not start a scan.

A watched device logs an event when it goes quiet and when it comes back. Other devices do not, because phones and laptops would fill the log. See Get told when a device goes quiet.

items.title: The change log
items.text: The Events page lists every change: new devices, addresses added and removed, new names, ports opened and closed, type changes, and your own edits. Notifications send these events to other services.

items.title: What you own
items.text:
The label, group, type, notes, ignored flag and watched flag are yours. Scans never change them. See Label, group and ignore devices.

If you do not give a device a type, Jocasta guesses one. See How a device gets its type.

items.title: Retention
items.text:
Record Kept for Setting Change log and scans 90 days retention.history Hourly traffic totals 30 days retention.traffic Hourly DNS lookup counts 30 days retention.dns Devices you never touched, after last seen 90 days retention.devices

0s keeps a record forever.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• An open port is a port that accepted a TCP connection. Jocasta guesses the service name from the port number.
  • If a device has no recorded ports, port scanning can be off.
  • Traffic shows only what passed the router while flow export was on.
  • Jocasta names an internet address after the network that announces it. For a cloud address, that is the provider.

items.title: Configure
items.text:
No setting is required. If networks is empty, Jocasta sweeps the network of the host's default route. It does this only if the network is a /22 or smaller. All other settings have a default. jocasta.example.yaml lists every setting, with its default and a line about what it does. The configuration reference gives the type, allowed values and environment variable of each setting.

Jocasta reads settings in this order. Each one overrides the one before it:

  1. built-in defaults
  2. a YAML file, jocasta.yaml in the working directory, or the path given to --config
  3. environment variables prefixed JOCASTA_

In an environment variable, a double underscore separates levels. A single underscore stays part of the key:

JOCASTA_SCAN__DEVICES__INTERVAL=10m      # scan.devices.interval
JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD=change-me

Jocasta shows times in the time zone of the server. In a container, this time zone is UTC. To see local times, set your time zone. This setting changes only how Jocasta shows times. It always stores them in UTC.

location:
  timezone: "Australia/Sydney"   # an IANA zone name

Jocasta deletes a device when no scan has seen it for 90 days. It does not delete a device that you labelled, grouped, typed, noted, ignored or watched. Each time a phone changes its privacy address, it leaves one such device. To change the window, set retention.devices. To keep every device, set it to 0:

retention:
  devices: "2160h"

Do not commit a jocasta.yaml that holds real addresses or credentials to a repository.

items.title: What to turn on next
items.text:
• Port scanning: to probe every known address on your networks for open TCP ports at a set interval, set scan.ports.enabled: true. Jocasta also probes each address on the TCP ports on which its device advertises a service. For a single scan, see CLI.
  • Routers: devices on every VLAN, and what is connected where. See Plugins.
  • Traffic: who each device talks to, from the flow exports of your router. It adds a Traffic page and a live Map. See NetFlow and Tour the web UI.
  • DNS lookups: what each device looks up, from the query log of your resolver. See Record what devices look up.
  • Notifications: new devices, opened ports and other changes. Jocasta sends them to ntfy, a signed webhook, or any service that accepts an HTTP request. See Notifications.
  • MCP server: AI agents can query the inventory. See MCP server.
  • JSON API: under /api, for scripts and dashboards. See JSON API.

items.title: Make targets
items.text:
make build          # build to bin/
make test           # go test ./...
make e2e            # browser tests a pull request must pass (needs Chrome)
make e2e-full       # browser tests on every screen and account
make smoke          # read the router, DNS and NetFlow sources in containers (needs Docker)
make lint           # golangci-lint (installs it to bin/ on first run)
make dev            # hot-reload server via air
make gen            # regenerate sqlc models
make new_migration name=<name>
make oui            # rebuild the embedded MAC-vendor table
make htmx           # refresh the vendored htmx
make docs           # build the docs site and check every link (needs uv)
make docs-serve     # preview the docs site at http://localhost:8000

items.title: Browser tests
items.text:
internal/web/e2e drives Chrome over the real server. It builds with the e2e tag, so go test ./... leaves it out. It needs Google Chrome or Chromium on PATH, or E2E_CHROME set to one of them.

The tests draw each page over four fabricated inventories: empty, a home network, a network with extreme data, and a network with no accounts. They also draw each dialog, menu and inline edit that the page opens. Each drawing is checked for these problems:

  • sideways scrolling
  • clipped or overlapping text
  • small tap targets and small text
  • WCAG 2.2 AA failures (axe-core)
  • script errors and failed requests

make e2e draws every page as admin on a phone, a tablet and a laptop, in both themes. It takes about two minutes. CI does not run it. So run it before you open a pull request that changes the UI. make e2e-full adds every other screen and account. scripts/release.sh runs it before it tags a release.

A finding fails the run, unless testdata/known.json lists it under an open issue. A fix deletes its entries. make e2e-full also fails on an entry that no longer matches a finding.

The run also compares the first screen of every page on the home network with a stored picture in testdata/golden/. It does this on a phone, a tablet and a laptop in the light theme, and on the laptop in the dark theme. A picture fails when more than 64 of its pixels changed. One added or removed word changes more pixels than that. If you change the UI on purpose, store the new pictures and commit them with the change:

E2E_UPDATE=1 make e2e

To see what changed, set E2E_ARTIFACTS to a directory. The run writes each picture that differs there, next to a map of the changed pixels.

To look at a fixture in a browser:

E2E_SERVE=weird go test -tags e2e -run TestServe -timeout 0 ./internal/web/e2e/

To capture every page and read the findings, without a pass or fail:

E2E_AUDIT=$PWD/tmp/audit TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp go test -tags e2e -run TestAudit -timeout 0 ./internal/web/e2e/

To limit either run, set E2E_FIXTURES, E2E_ROLES, E2E_VIEWPORTS, E2E_THEMES or E2E_PAGES to a comma-separated list.

items.title: Smoke tests
items.text:
make smoke reads real OpenWrt, RouterOS, Pi-hole, AdGuard Home and Technitium servers and a real NetFlow exporter, each in a container. It checks what jocasta says about them. The plugin tests use canned replies. The smoke tests find a server that changed what it sends. They need Docker and Go. CI does not run them. So run them before you open a pull request that changes one of these plugins or its client under pkg/.

scripts/smoke/smoke.sh up starts the servers on their own network, 198.51.100.0/24:

  • OpenWrt has the setup that the OpenWrt page gives, with the ACL in docs/openwrt/jocasta.json. It also gets leases and static hosts.
  • RouterOS CHR runs in QEMU, and scripts/smoke/routeros.sh boots it. Its ether1 gets an address over DHCP, as a WAN port does. Its ether2 is on the smoke network. It gets a read-only jocasta user, a bridge with its own address, a DHCP server with a static lease, and a static ARP entry. It also gets Traffic Flow that exports IPFIX, with the setup from the RouterOS page.
  • Pi-hole, AdGuard Home and Technitium each block a name. AdGuard Home also rewrites one name. Technitium has the setup that the Technitium page gives: a user that can view Logs, its API token, and the Query Logs (Sqlite) app. Pi-hole is the upstream of the other two, so no lookup leaves the network.
  • pmacct runs in the network namespace of the OpenWrt container. It exports NetFlow v9 to this host, as the router would.
  • The OpenWrt container sends lookups to each resolver.

Each server publishes its web interface on 127.0.0.1, and jocasta reads it there.

scripts/smoke/smoke.sh check runs jocasta plugin run against each server and checks the rows that it prints. It also runs these tests:

  • TestNetFlowLive in internal/plugin, two times. The first time, the OpenWrt container makes a lookup. The second time, this host makes a request to the router. The script checks the flows that each run decodes.
  • The live tests in pkg/openwrt, pkg/routeros and internal/plugin.

The script writes its config to $TMPDIR/jocasta-smoke/jocasta.yaml. So you can point jocasta serve at the same servers. make smoke-down removes the servers.

Some services need more than Docker. To leave a service out, add it to SMOKE_SKIP, such as SMOKE_SKIP="technitium netflow" make smoke:

  • routeros: RouterOS runs under QEMU. If the host has no KVM, QEMU emulates the CPU. In both cases, it boots in less than a minute. Its container joins a second network, which needs Docker 28 or later.
  • technitium: the server downloads the Query Logs app from the app store of Technitium. So its container needs internet access.
  • netflow: the exporter sends to the gateway address of the network. Only Docker on Linux puts this address on the host.

To change a setting, set the matching variable:

  • SMOKE_REGISTRY pulls the images from a mirror, such as mirror.gcr.io. Use it when Docker Hub limits your pulls.
  • SMOKE_PIHOLE_IMAGE, SMOKE_ADGUARD_IMAGE, SMOKE_OPENWRT_IMAGE, SMOKE_ROUTEROS_IMAGE, SMOKE_TECHNITIUM_IMAGE and SMOKE_PMACCT_IMAGE test a different release. MikroTik publishes no image. The RouterOS image is evilfreelancer/docker-routeros, which contains the CHR disk and QEMU.
  • SMOKE_PIHOLE_PORT, SMOKE_ADGUARD_PORT, SMOKE_ADGUARD_SETUP_PORT, SMOKE_OPENWRT_PORT, SMOKE_TECHNITIUM_PORT and SMOKE_ROUTEROS_PORT change the published ports, 18081 to 18086 by default. SMOKE_FLOW_PORT and SMOKE_ROUTEROS_FLOW_PORT change the ports for the NetFlow and IPFIX exports, 2055 and 2056 by default.

netifd cannot create the br-lan bridge in a container. So the lan of the OpenWrt container is on eth0. Its bridge table and VLANs are empty. The unit tests cover the reads of these tables.

items.title: Docs
items.text:
Zensical publishes the pages in docs/ to GitHub Pages. There is one version for each minor release and one for main. The Docs workflow builds every pull request that changes the docs with make docs. This build fails on a broken link or anchor. A merge to main publishes the dev version. A v* tag publishes its minor version as latest. The Zensical fork of mike pushes both to the gh-pages branch.

When you change the docs:

  • Add a new page to nav in mkdocs.yml, and to the llmstxt sections there. If you do not, the site leaves it out of the sidebar and llms.txt.
  • A new plugin gets a page under docs/plugins/ and a line in the table on the plugins overview. A DNS resolver also gets a column on Record what devices look up.
  • A new setting gets a row in the configuration reference. TestReferenceDocumentsEveryKey fails until the setting has a row. It also fails on a row for a setting that no longer exists.
  • Keep docs/setup.md and docs/mcp.md. Earlier releases link to their sections on GitHub. Each section there points to the new location.

items.title: Release
items.text:
After CI passes on main, run the command below. It runs make e2e-full first, so Chrome must be installed.

./scripts/release.sh v0.10.0

The script needs a clean working tree and a local main that matches origin/main. It checks that the tag is not used. Then it creates an annotated tag and pushes it, which starts the release workflow. It does not wait for the build.

git-cliff writes the GitHub release and the changelog page from the commit messages, as cliff.toml sets. To give a minor release highlights, merge docs/releases/<major.minor>.md before you tag its .0.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
• cmd/jocasta: CLI entry point.
  • internal/scanner: the ICMP sweep, and the reverse DNS, mDNS, NetBIOS, DNS-SD and SSDP lookups that name the hosts that answer.
  • internal/plugin: sources other than the sweep (RouterOS, OpenWrt, NetFlow, Technitium, Pi-hole, AdGuard Home).
  • internal/inventory: the store. It covers identity resolution, address handling, device classification and the change log.
  • internal/classify: the rules that guess the type of a device from its vendor, name and open ports.
  • internal/notify: sends the changes of each finished scan to ntfy, a webhook or a templated HTTP request.
  • internal/web, internal/api: the HTML UI and the JSON API.
  • internal/db: connection, migrations, generated queries.

SQLC generates the queries from internal/db/queries/. The schema is in internal/db/migrations/.

items.title: Add a notification service
items.text:
Most services accept an HTTP request. The http provider reaches them with a body template and no new code. For such a service, add a recipe to Send to another service. TestRecipesInTheDocsRender renders every recipe on that page. So a broken recipe fails the tests.

A service gets its own provider only when the http provider cannot reach it. For example, the service needs more than one request, a protocol other than HTTP, or a signature that a template cannot make. Each provider is in its own file in internal/notify, as ntfy.go and webhook.go are:

  1. Add a struct with koanf tags for its settings. Give it Validate, Host and Send. Send must not put a credential in its error. For a service that accepts an HTTP request, use post.
  2. Add a field for it to notify.Config, and a line to Config.provider.
  3. Add an example to jocasta.example.yaml. Add a row for each setting to the configuration reference.

The notifier, the settings page, the store and cmd need no change.

items.title: Add a name source
items.text:
Each name has a standing, dbtype.HostnameSource, which tells how Jocasta learned it. If sources give different names, Jocasta shows the name with the higher standing.

  1. Add a constant for it in internal/db/dbtype/enum.go, and add it to hostnameSources.
  2. Give it a place in HostnameSource.Rank. Give the reason in the comment there. A name that resolves ranks above a name that a device only claims.
  3. Write its device page text in standing, in internal/web/funcs.go.
  4. List it in Name devices.

If a sweep asks devices for their names, do two more steps:

  1. Add its lookup in its own file in internal/scanner. Ask it in enrich, in rank order. A query that goes to each host is a nameProtocol, as in mdns.go and netbios.go. Any other lookup is a nameLookup, as askSSDP in ssdp.go is. Or it names hosts itself, as browseServices does with dnssd.go.
  2. Add it to HostnameSource.Swept. Then a lookup with a lower rank never replaces its name on the claim of the sweep.

The column has no CHECK, so a new standing needs no migration.

items.title: Screenshots
items.text: The images in docs/ui.md come from a database of fabricated devices, never real network data: addresses from RFC 5737, hardware addresses from RFC 7042, and invented names. The internet peers are well-known public services, so Jocasta can find their organisations and countries.

items.title: Label, group and ignore devices
items.text:
These fields are yours. Scans never change them. They stay with the device when its address or name changes. To edit them, you need an Admin or Editor account.

  • Label: the name that Jocasta shows everywhere. Up to 200 characters.
  • Group: puts devices together, such as Office. You can filter the device list by group. Up to 100 characters.
  • Type: sets the icon. Auto keeps Jocasta's guess. See How a device gets its type.
  • Notes: free text. Up to 2,000 characters.
  • Ignored: hides the device from lists and counts.
  • Watched: logs an event when the device goes quiet or comes back. See Get told when a device goes quiet.

items.title: Edit a device
items.text:
1. In Devices, select the device.
  2. Select Edit details.
  3. Change the fields.
  4. Select Save.

If you leave a field empty, Jocasta clears it. The change log records each edit.

To change only the label and group, select the pencil at the end of the row in the device list.

items.title: Ignore a device
items.text:
Ignore a device that you know and never want to see, such as a neighbour's printer:

  1. In Edit details, tick Ignore this device.
  2. Select Save.

The sweep still records the device. The port scan skips it, and notifications leave it out. To see it again, select Show ignored in the device list filters.

items.title: From a script or an agent
items.text: Use PATCH /api/devices/{id} in the JSON API, or the update_device_curation tool in the MCP server. Both need a read_write token. The MCP prompt triage_devices suggests a label, group and type for each device that has none.

items.title: Install
items.text: For a guided first run, see Your first inventory.

items.title: Container image
items.text:
Images for amd64 and arm64 are on the GitHub Container Registry. Each image has the tag latest and a release tag, such as :v0.11.1. The image is distroless and does not run as root. It listens on 0.0.0.0:8080, keeps its database in /data, and reads /data/jocasta.yaml.

docker runCompose 
docker run -d --name jocasta --network host \
  -v jocasta-data:/data \
  -v ./jocasta.yaml:/data/jocasta.yaml:ro \
  ghcr.io/pushkar-anand/jocasta:latest

services:
  jocasta:
    image: ghcr.io/pushkar-anand/jocasta:latest
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - jocasta-data:/data
      - ./jocasta.yaml:/data/jocasta.yaml:ro

volumes:
  jocasta-data:

Use host networking. On a bridge network (-p 8080:8080), the sweep finds hosts but not their hardware addresses. Also, mDNS, DNS-SD and SSDP names do not arrive. A router plugin can supply the hardware addresses. Neither mode needs extra capabilities.

Host networking reaches your network only on Linux. On macOS and Windows, Docker runs containers in a VM, so use the prebuilt binary.

items.title: Prebuilt binaries
items.text:
Archives for Linux, macOS and Windows, on amd64 and arm64, are on the releases page. A checksums.txt file is with them.

  1. Extract jocasta from the archive for your system.
  2. Put a jocasta.yaml next to it.
  3. From that directory, run jocasta serve. It does not need root.

It listens on localhost:8080. To reach it from other machines, set server.host: 0.0.0.0.

items.title: From source
items.text:
You need Go 1.27 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/pushkar-anand/jocasta.git
cd jocasta
make build            # -> bin/jocasta
make docker           # -> jocasta:latest

items.title: First run
items.text:
On the first visit, Jocasta asks you to create the admin account. Until this account exists, anyone who reaches the page can create it. So create it immediately. To add more users, see Manage users and sign-in.

To sign in over plain HTTP, set server.auth.cookie_secure: false. See Serve over HTTPS.

Jocasta runs database migrations when it starts. Before you upgrade, see Back up and upgrade.

items.title: How names are chosen
items.text:
More than one source can name a device. Jocasta shows the name from the source with the highest rank in this list. If you give a device a label, Jocasta shows the label instead of all of these names. See Label, group and ignore devices.

  1. Reverse DNS. Jocasta looks it up for each address that a sweep finds.
  2. A static DHCP lease on your router.
  3. mDNS. Jocasta asks each address that the sweep finds and that has no reverse DNS name.
  4. A dynamic DHCP lease on your router.
  5. NetBIOS. Jocasta asks each address that the sweep finds and that has no name from reverse DNS or mDNS.
  6. DNS-SD. If an address still has no name, Jocasta uses the name that it gives the services it advertises.
  7. SSDP. If an address still has no name, Jocasta uses the label in its UPnP description.

If two names of the same rank are different, the device keeps its current name while a source still gives that name. If no source gives it, the device takes the name that Jocasta heard last.

A device can have several addresses, such as a router with an address on each VLAN. Each address can give a name. The device keeps one of these names. It does not change to the name of the address that Jocasta read last. The device page lists the name that each source gives for each address.

Jocasta does not use the reverse DNS names that systemd-resolved makes up, such as _gateway.

When a sweep has a name for a device, a lookup with a lower rank does not replace it. The device keeps that name until a lookup with the same or a higher rank gives a different name.

items.title: mDNS
items.text:
mDNS names phones, TVs, printers and computers that reverse DNS does not know, such as living-room-tv.local. Jocasta sends one query to each such device, on UDP port 5353. This query does not need host networking or multicast. As the mDNS standard asks, most devices answer only a query from their own segment. So devices on other segments rarely get an mDNS name.

To turn mDNS off, set scan.devices.resolve_mdns: false. It does not depend on scan.devices.resolve_names. If reverse DNS is off, no device has a reverse DNS name. Then Jocasta asks every device that answers the sweep over mDNS.

items.title: NetBIOS
items.text: NetBIOS names Windows computers and devices that run Samba, such as a NAS. A NetBIOS name, such as DESKTOP-4F2K, has at most 15 characters. Jocasta sends one query, on UDP port 137, to each device that still has no name. Windows answers only when file and printer sharing is on. By default, it answers only a query from its own segment. To turn NetBIOS off, set scan.devices.resolve_netbios: false.

items.title: DNS-SD
items.text:
DNS-SD names TVs, speakers, printers and other devices that advertise their services over mDNS but do not answer an mDNS query for their own name.

After each sweep, Jocasta asks the multicast group 224.0.0.251:5353 which service types are on the segment. Then it asks which devices offer each type. A Google Cast device gets the name that its owner gave it in the Home app, such as Living Room TV. Any other device gets the name that most of its services share. Jocasta does not use a name that is only a serial number or another ID.

Jocasta binds UDP port 5353 to hear the answers. It shares this port with any mDNS responder on the same machine, such as Avahi. Like SSDP, DNS-SD reaches only Jocasta's own segment, and only with host networking. To turn it off, set scan.devices.resolve_dnssd: false.

Jocasta also records the services that each device advertises, with or without a name. The Ports table on the device page lists the services that the latest sweep heard.

The port scan probes each advertised TCP port, so the table shows whether the port answers. The scan also probes every port that it recorded as open. So when a service moves to a new port, its old port closes. A port that the scan probes only because a device advertised it opens and closes without an event. This is because a phone advertises on a new random port each time.

The classifier reads every service that a sweep heard within retention.history. So if one sweep misses an answer, the device's type does not change. For example, a print service marks a printer, and the Android TV remote service marks a TV. If no sweep heard a service within retention.history, Jocasta deletes it.

items.title: SSDP
items.text:
SSDP names TVs, speakers, media players, printers and routers that no other source names. The name is the label that the device shows its owner, such as Living Room TV.

If a sweep leaves a device without a name, Jocasta sends one SSDP search to the multicast group 239.255.255.250:1900. A device that answers points to its UPnP description. For each device that still has no name, Jocasta gets that description and takes the friendlyName from it. It gets the description only from the address that answered, over plain HTTP. It reads at most 64 KB and waits at most 2 seconds.

The search reaches only Jocasta's own segment, and only with host networking, because a bridge network does not pass multicast. To turn SSDP off, set scan.devices.resolve_ssdp: false.

items.title: Your first inventory
items.text:
In this tutorial, you run Jocasta in a container and sweep your network. Then you name a device and get a message on your phone when it goes quiet. It takes about 10 minutes.

This tutorial runs Jocasta in Docker on a Linux machine on your network. On macOS or Windows, run the binary instead. Docker there runs containers in a VM, so the sweep does not reach your network.

items.title: 1. Write the config
items.text:
Create jocasta.yaml in an empty directory:

server:
  auth:
    cookie_secure: false   # sign in over plain HTTP

Jocasta sweeps the network of the host. To sweep other networks, list them under networks. See Configure.

items.title: 2. Start Jocasta
items.text:
docker run -d --name jocasta --network host \
  -v jocasta-data:/data \
  -v ./jocasta.yaml:/data/jocasta.yaml:ro \
  ghcr.io/pushkar-anand/jocasta:latest

With host networking, the sweep can read hardware addresses.

items.title: 3. Create the admin account
items.text:
Open http://<host>:8080. Enter a username and a password of 8 or more characters, and select Create admin account.

Until this account exists, anyone who reaches the page can create it. So do this step immediately.

items.title: 4. Look at the first sweep
items.text:
The first sweep runs when Jocasta starts. Open Devices. Each row is one device, with its addresses, vendor and name.

A row with no vendor is usually a phone or a laptop. These devices make up their hardware address. A row with no name is a device that did not answer a name lookup.

items.title: 5. Name a device
items.text:
1. Select a device you recognise.
  2. Select Edit details.
  3. Set Label to Office printer and Group to Office.
  4. Select Save.

The device list shows the new label.

items.title: 6. Watch it
items.text:
On the device's page, select Watch.

A watched device goes quiet 15 minutes after the last scan that saw it. To test this, turn the device off for 20 minutes. Then open Events.

items.title: 7. Get a message on your phone
items.text:
1. Install ntfy on your phone and subscribe to a topic. Topics are public. So use a name that nobody can guess, such as jocasta-k3v9q2.

  2. Add it to jocasta.yaml:

    notify:
  phone:
    ntfy:
      url: "https://ntfy.sh/jocasta-k3v9q2"

  3. Restart Jocasta: docker restart jocasta.

  4. Open the account menu, top right, and select Notifications.
  5. Under phone, tick Watched device went quiet and Watched device came back.
  6. Select Save.
  7. Select Send test. Your phone gets the message "Jocasta test".

items.title: Next
items.text:
