  • Connect your router for devices on other VLANs
  • Serve over HTTPS

items.title: Tour the web UI
items.text:
This page shows each page of the web UI. The pages read the same data as the JSON API. The Overview, Map and Topology pages refresh themselves.

The screenshots below use synthetic data: addresses from RFC 5737, hardware addresses from RFC 7042, and invented names. The internet peers are well-known public services, so Jocasta can find their organisations.

items.title: Overview
items.text: Counts for each network, a presence summary, the last sweep, and recent changes.

items.title: Device list
items.text: Filter by group, network or presence. Search by name, address or vendor. The list hides ignored devices, unless you ask for them.

items.title: Device page
items.text:
Everything that Jocasta knows about one device:

  • Identity: what Jocasta found the device to be. It also shows whether Jocasta knows the device by its hardware address or only by its IP address.
  • What you call it: label, group, type and notes. No scan or plugin changes these.
  • Connected: the path from the internet to the device, through each router, switch and access point. Each step shows the port or Wi-Fi network, the band and the VLAN. If the device connects directly to a port that Jocasta reads, the page shows the link rate. For a Wi-Fi client, it shows the rate in each direction and the signal. If a wired link runs slower than both ends can, the page tells you. Show on topology opens the Topology page on the device.
  • Addresses: every address that the device had, and the network of each address.
  • Ports: the TCP ports that the device listens on, and the ports that it closed since. This section shows only after a port scan reached the device. See CLI.
  • Sources: the name that each source, such as the sweep or the router, gives the device at each address. It also shows when Jocasta last heard from each source.
  • History: the entries for the device in the change log.

items.title: Talks to
items.text:
If traffic collection is set up, this section shows who the device exchanged data with. You can show the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days. See NetFlow.

The top of the section shows the data received and sent. It also shows the number of peers on your network and of organisations on the internet. Below that, there is one tab for each network segment and one for the internet. Each tab has a count. The busiest tab opens first.

On the tab of a segment, each peer is one row, for all the services on which the device reached it. If the peer is a device, the row links to its page. Addresses that no device has collapse into one row for each subnet. The Internet tab groups addresses by the organisation that announces them. Use the search box and the filters to show one service only, or to search by name, address or organisation.

Each row shows who opened its connections. "→ 12" means that the device opened 12. "← 3" means that the peer opened 3. A row can show both. The direction filter shows one side only.

Something on the internet can try to reach the device without exchanging data, such as a knock on a forwarded port. In that case, a note shows how many addresses tried, from how many organisations, and on which ports. Jocasta counts tries on the outside address of the router under the router. Jocasta learns that address from the flows themselves.

The device can start connections that carry no data, such as a refused port, a port that nobody answered, or a ping. Jocasta counts these at the top and does not show them in the tabs. To add them, tick "Show tries with no data". Each try then goes in the row of its peer, with the number that got an answer and the ports tried. If the tries add up to probing of the network, a notice at the top tells you.

The Broadcasts tab lists the packets that the device sent to a whole subnet or multicast group. Most of these are discovery protocols, such as mDNS, SSDP, DHCP or a sync tool that looks for its peers. Jocasta guesses the names from the port and group.

items.title: Traffic page
items.text:
If traffic collection is set up, this page shows a summary of the whole network. You can show the last 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days. These are its cards:

  • Probing your network: devices that tried 20 or more addresses within an hour without exchanging data. Also devices that tried 20 or more ports on one address in this way. A device that you run scans from also shows here.
  • Reached from the internet: each device and service that something on the internet connected to. This card leaves out a service that uses the same port at both ends, such as a VPN server on IKE. Its clients look like replies.
  • Probed from the internet: connections from the internet that carried no data, for each device and for the outside address of the router.
  • Busiest devices and Top internet destinations. Each organisation opens to show the devices behind it.
  • New this week: organisations that a device first exchanged data with in the last 7 days.

There is a tab for each network segment. A tab shows every card for the devices of that segment only, with its totals at the top. You can also show one group only.

The outside address of the router can itself be private. This happens when the carrier-grade NAT of the ISP, or another router, is in front of it. If so, the page tells you. Then nothing on the internet can connect in over IPv4, so the two internet cards stay empty.

items.title: Map
items.text:
If traffic collection is set up, the Map shows the traffic of the last hour as a tree. It redraws every minute, because Jocasta records new traffic every minute.

  • The router is in the middle, with a hub for each network and one for the internet.
  • Devices and organisations spread out around their hub. The Map shows the 60 busiest devices and the 12 busiest organisations.
  • A branch is thicker when more traffic passed along it. It moves if something under it was active in the last 15 minutes.
  • A faint line joins each device to what it exchanged traffic with: an organisation, or a device on another network. Traffic between two devices on the same network never passes the router, so the Map does not show it.
  • The legend in the top right gives the colour of each network, with its device count. Point at a network to show its devices.

Click a device or organisation to highlight its lines. The Map then names the services on each line ("https", "mqtts", "port 123 UDP") and dims everything else. Click the device again to open its page. To go back, click the empty map or press Escape.

To zoom, scroll or pinch. To pan, drag. To zoom in on a spot, double-click it. The search box dims everything that does not match. Enter zooms to the first match. The Map keeps the view, the search and the place of each device when it redraws.

items.title: World
items.text:
The World tab shows the same internet traffic of the last hour on a map of the world.

  • A country is darker when more traffic went to addresses registered there. A marker pulses on the countries that were active in the last 15 minutes.
  • A line goes from the country of your network to each of the others. It is thicker when it carried more traffic, and it moves while it is active.
  • Click a country to see the devices and organisations behind its traffic. The search finds countries by name.

The country of your network comes from the outside address of the router. If that address is private, it comes from location.country. See NetFlow.

A country is where an address is registered. For a big provider, this is often its home country. The server itself can be in a different country.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
The Topology page shows the network from the internet down. It redraws every minute. See Show what is plugged in where.

  • The internet is at the top, with the router below it. Each switch and access point hangs from the port that it is connected to. A thick line is a trunk. A thin line carries one VLAN. A dashed line is Wi-Fi.
  • Under each box, the page groups its wired devices by VLAN, with the port of each device on the right. It groups its Wi-Fi devices by network, with the band of each device.
  • A solid box is a device that Jocasta reads. A dashed box is a device that only announced itself to a device that Jocasta reads. Jocasta infers a dotted box when several devices share one port behind it. If one of these devices is a hypervisor, the box is that device. The others are its virtual machines. To mark a host that Jocasta did not recognise, set its type to Hypervisor on its page. If most devices in a dotted box have the hardware address of a virtual machine, the box has the label Hypervisor.
  • A quiet device stays where Jocasta last saw it, dimmed. Some devices are seen recently, but no router, switch or access point saw them on a port. The page lists them under the tree.
  • The legend in the top right gives the colour of each VLAN, with its device count. Point at a VLAN to show its devices.

Click a device to highlight the path from the internet down to it. Click it again to open its page. Search, zoom and pan work as on the Map.

items.title: Network page
items.text: One segment, its VLAN tag and name, and the devices on it.

items.title: Events
items.text: The full change log.

items.title: Light theme
items.text: A toggle in the header changes the theme. Each browser keeps its own choice.

items.title: JSON API
items.text: Jocasta serves its inventory as JSON under /api, for scripts and dashboards. The API uses the same API tokens as the MCP server.

items.title: Authenticate
items.text:
Create an API token and send it with each request:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://<host>:8080/api/devices

A read token can make only GET requests. A read_write token can also change devices. A token never expires, unless you selected 30 days, 90 days or 1 year when you created it. Jocasta refuses an expired token, as it refuses a revoked token. The expired token stays in the list until you revoke it.

For health checks, GET /api/livez answers without a token.

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
Request Returns GET /api/livez Whether the server is up. GET /api/stats Counts across the inventory. GET /api/groups The device groups in use. GET /api/devices The device list. GET /api/devices/{id} One device. PATCH /api/devices/{id} Changes a device's label, group, type, notes or ignored flag. Needs a read_write token. PATCH /api/devices/{id}/watch Starts or stops watching a device. Needs a read_write token. GET /api/devices/{id}/events A device's change log. GET /api/devices/{id}/traffic Who a device talked to. Needs traffic recorded. GET /api/devices/{id}/dns What a device looked up. Needs lookups recorded. GET /api/events The change log across all devices. GET /api/scans Past scans.

Jocasta returns an error as an RFC 9457 problem document. Its title and detail tell you what to change.

items.title: Browser access
items.text: A page on another origin can read /api only if server.cors.allowed_origins lists its origin. See the configuration reference.

items.title: MCP server
items.text:
Jocasta can serve the inventory to AI agents, such as Claude Code, over the Model Context Protocol. By default, the MCP server is off.

An agent connected this way can answer questions such as:

  • What joined the network this week?
  • Which devices have SSH open?
  • What is 192.0.2.47, and when was it first seen?
  • Which devices talked to a new organisation today?

With a read_write token, the agent can also label and group devices. It reads what past scans recorded. It never starts a scan.

items.title: Turn it on
items.text:
1. Set server.mcp.enabled: true in the config file, or JOCASTA_SERVER__MCP__ENABLED=true. While the MCP server is off, /mcp answers 404.
  2. Create an API token. See API tokens. A read token gets only the tools that read the inventory. A read_write token also gets the tools that change it.

The endpoint is /mcp. It uses the Streamable HTTP transport. Send the token as Authorization: Bearer <token>. When a client connects, it finds the available tools and prompts.

The devices themselves report their hostnames and vendor names. So any device on your network can choose what an agent reads in these fields. Give an agent a read token, unless it must change something.

items.title: Connect a client
items.text:
The examples use https://jocasta.example.test/mcp. Replace it with the address of your server.

Claude Code

claude mcp add --transport http jocasta https://jocasta.example.test/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer <token>"

Codex

Codex reads the token from an environment variable. So the token is not in its config file:

export JOCASTA_TOKEN=<token>
codex mcp add jocasta --url https://jocasta.example.test/mcp \
  --bearer-token-env-var JOCASTA_TOKEN

Hermes Agent

  1. Put JOCASTA_TOKEN=<token> in ~/.hermes/.env.

  2. Add the server to ~/.hermes/config.yaml:

    mcp_servers:
  jocasta:
    url: "https://jocasta.example.test/mcp"
    headers:
      Authorization: "Bearer ${JOCASTA_TOKEN}"

  3. In a running session, run /reload-mcp.

Other clients

Any client works if it supports Streamable HTTP and lets you set a request header. Some clients can only start a local server over stdio. For these clients, a bridge such as mcp-remote can forward to the endpoint.

items.title: Tools
items.text: Tool What it answers list_devices Which devices match a search, group, network, type, presence (seen recently or quiet) or whether you watch them. get_device Everything about one device: addresses, ports, advertised services, sources, your labels, and where it is plugged in and how fast. explain_device Why a device has the class it has: the facts the classifier used, the rule that decided and every other rule that matched. list_events What changed, across the network or for one device. list_networks, get_network The network segments, and how many devices are on each. list_groups The groups you filed devices under. get_stats How many devices were seen recently, are quiet, are ignored or were discovered in the last 24 hours. get_port_overview Open ports across the network, and the commonest services. list_scans When scans ran, and what they found. list_traffic Who devices exchanged data with. Needs traffic collection. list_dns The names a device looked up, and which were blocked. Needs lookups recorded. get_topology What is plugged in where, and how fast each link runs. Needs topology set up. update_device_curation Sets a device's label, group, type, notes and ignored flag. read_write tokens only. watch_device Watches a device, or stops, so you are told when it goes quiet or comes back. read_write tokens only.

items.title: Prompts
items.text:
A prompt is a saved procedure that you start yourself. The agent then does the procedure with the tools. In Claude Code, prompts show as slash commands, such as /mcp__jocasta__weekly_report.

Prompt What it does triage_devices Finds the devices that need attention: unlabelled, doubtfully classified, or likely duplicates left by a randomised hardware address. Proposes a label, group and type for each. With a read_write token the agent applies the proposals you confirm; with a read token it only proposes. weekly_report Summarises what changed over the last 7 days: new devices, devices gone quiet, organisations a device reached for the first time (when traffic collection is set up), port changes, identity changes, and what may need a look. Takes an optional days argument, from 1 to 90. It can reach back only as far as retention.history keeps the change log.

items.title: Errors
items.text: An error is an RFC 9457 problem document, as in the HTTP API. A failed tool call returns this document as the text of an error result. The instance field has the tool name. Jocasta writes the cause of a 500 only to the server log.

items.title: Notifications
items.text:
Jocasta can send the changes from each scan to these destinations:

  • an ntfy topic
  • your own URL, as a signed JSON POST

  • any service that accepts an HTTP request, such as Discord, Slack or Telegram. See Send to another service.

  • Under notify in the config file, add each destination by name. Give each destination one service block:

notify:
  phone:
    ntfy:
      url: "https://ntfy.example.com/jocasta"   # the topic's address, as ntfy shows it
      token: ""                                 # or JOCASTA_NOTIFY__PHONE__NTFY__TOKEN
  automation:
    webhook:
      url: "https://hooks.example.com/jocasta"
      secret: "change-me"                       # required; signs each request

A destination is on, unless it has enabled: false. 2. Restart Jocasta, so that it reads the change. 3. Open the account menu at the top right, and select Notifications. 4. For each destination, tick the kinds of change to send to it. 5. Select Save. 6. Optional: select Send test. The destination gets a message with the title "Jocasta test".

Jocasta sends one message for each scan that changes something, such as "2 new devices on 192.0.2.0/24". In the first scan of a network, every device is new. So Jocasta sends only a count for that scan ("Found 42 devices"). Jocasta does not send changes to devices that you ignore, or your own edits. If Jocasta cannot deliver a message, it logs the failure and shows it on the Notifications page. It does not send the message again.

The configuration reference lists every notify setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: Send to another service
items.text:
The http service posts each message with a body that you write as a template. So it can reach any service that accepts an HTTP request. Find the recipe for your service below, and copy it under notify.

The body is a Go template. The template gets these values and functions:

  • .Title and .Body: the title of the message, such as "2 new devices on 192.0.2.0/24", and its text, with one change on each line.
  • .ScanID: the scan that the changes came from. It is 0 for a test.
  • .Events: each change, with .Kind, .DeviceID, .Device and .Change.
  • json: writes a value as JSON, with quotes and escapes. Use it for every value in a JSON body, as {{ json .Title }}. Device names can contain quotes, and the body contains line breaks.
  • truncate: cuts a string to a number of characters and adds … at the end, as {{ .Body | truncate 2000 | json }}. A message lists up to 20 changes. Long device names can make it longer than the limit of a service. The service then returns an error.

Jocasta sends the body as application/json, unless headers sets a different Content-Type. When Jocasta starts, it renders the template with two sample messages. One sample has a change. The other is the test message, which has no change. If the template does not parse, or its output is not valid JSON, Jocasta reports the problem and does not start.

A device gives its own name. So its name can contain text that a chat service reads as a mention, such as @everyone, or as formatting. The Slack, Telegram, Gotify, Pushover and Apprise recipes send plain text. Discord has no plain-text mode. So its recipe turns mentions off, but a device name can still show with formatting.

Discord, with the webhook URL from the Integrations settings of the channel:

discord:
  http:
    url: "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/<id>/<token>"
    body: '{"content": {{ printf "%s\n%s" .Title .Body | truncate 2000 | json }}, "allowed_mentions": {"parse": []}}'

Slack, with an incoming webhook URL. The message goes in a plain_text block, which Slack shows as it is. The recipe also sends the title as text, which Slack shows in its notifications:

slack:
  http:
    url: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/<path>"
    body: '{"text": {{ json .Title }}, "blocks": [{"type": "section", "text": {"type": "plain_text", "text": {{ printf "%s\n%s" .Title .Body | truncate 3000 | json }}}}]}'

Telegram, with the token of a bot and the chat to post in:

telegram:
  http:
    url: "https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/sendMessage"
    body: '{"chat_id": "<chat id>", "text": {{ printf "%s\n%s" .Title .Body | truncate 4096 | json }}}'

Gotify, with the token of an application:

gotify:
  http:
    url: "https://gotify.example.com/message"
    headers:
      X-Gotify-Key: "<app token>"
    body: '{"title": {{ json .Title }}, "message": {{ json .Body }}, "priority": 5}'

Pushover, with the token of an application and your user key:

pushover:
  http:
    url: "https://api.pushover.net/1/messages.json"
    body: '{"token": "<app token>", "user": "<user key>", "title": {{ json .Title }}, "message": {{ .Body | truncate 1024 | json }}}'

For email, SMS, Microsoft Teams, Signal and many more, run an Apprise API server next to Jocasta. In Apprise, save the Apprise URLs of the services under a key. Then post to that key:

apprise:
  http:
    url: "http://apprise.example.com:8000/notify/jocasta"
    body: '{"title": {{ json .Title }}, "body": {{ json .Body }}}'

Home Assistant, n8n and Node-RED accept any JSON, so they use the webhook service. For Home Assistant, add an automation with a webhook trigger. Then set the url of a webhook destination to the webhook of that automation. Home Assistant does not check the signature, but you must still set a secret. The automation reads the message as trigger.json.title and trigger.json.message. It reads each change under trigger.json.events.

home_assistant:
  webhook:
    url: "http://homeassistant.local:8123/api/webhook/<webhook id>"
    secret: "change-me"

items.title: Get told when a device goes quiet
items.text:
Watch the devices that you want to hear about when they go away, such as a server, a NAS or a camera. A watched device goes quiet when no scan has seen it for longer than the online window. By default, the online window is 15 minutes. The device comes back when a scan sees it again. Phones and laptops go quiet and come back all day. So a device that you do not watch never logs these events.

  1. On the device's page, select Watch.
  2. Open the account menu at the top right, and select Notifications.
  3. For a destination, tick Watched device went quiet and Watched device came back.
  4. Select Save.

A message has a title such as "1 device went quiet on 192.0.2.0/24". It has a line such as "NAS went quiet after 18 minutes without an answer". The change log records both kinds of event, even when no destination gets them. To list the watched devices that are quiet now, filter the device list to Watched only and Quiet.

Only a scan that could see a device can mark it quiet. That scan is a sweep of a network where the device has an address, or a read of a router that lists the device. If no scan covers the network of a device, the device stays as it was last seen. If a router read fails before it ends, it marks no device quiet.

To change how long a device can stay unseen, set the online window. The online window also sets which devices the device list counts as seen recently:

inventory:
  online_window: "30m"
path: Get told when a device goes quiet

items.title: Check a webhook's signature
items.text:
A webhook request is a POST. Its JSON body has these fields:

  • title and message: the text of the notification.
  • scan_id: the scan the changes came from. It can be missing.
  • events: the changes. Each change has a kind. It can also have device_id, device and change.

The request has two headers:

  • X-Jocasta-Signature-256: sha256=, then the hex HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body. The key is the secret of the destination.
  • X-Jocasta-Delivery: a random ID for this request. Log it. If you already handled a delivery with this ID, discard the request.

To check a request, compute the HMAC over the body exactly as you got it. Do this before you parse the body. Then compare the result with the header in constant time. In Go:

mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(secret))
mac.Write(body)
want := "sha256=" + hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil))
ok := hmac.Equal([]byte(want), []byte(r.Header.Get("X-Jocasta-Signature-256")))

Reject the request when ok is false.

items.title: Back up and upgrade
items.text: Jocasta keeps all its data in one SQLite database: inventory, change log, traffic, accounts, tokens and notification choices. Back up this database and your config file.

items.title: Back up
items.text:
In the container, the database is /data/jocasta.db. Recent writes can be in jocasta.db-wal, next to it. So stop Jocasta and copy the whole directory:

docker stop jocasta
docker run --rm -v jocasta-data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  cp -a /data /backup/jocasta-backup
docker start jocasta

The copy contains password hashes and two-factor secrets. Keep it safe.

To restore:

  1. Stop Jocasta.
  2. Put the files back.
  3. Start Jocasta.

items.title: Upgrade
items.text:
Jocasta is pre-1.0. A release can change the config format or the schema with no upgrade path.

  1. Read the upgrade notes for every release after yours.
  2. Back up.
  3. Pull the new tag, such as :v0.11.1.
  4. Recreate the container.

Jocasta updates the schema when it starts.

items.title: Downgrade
items.text: Restore the backup from before the upgrade. If you start an older release on a newer database, it migrates the schema down. This deletes the newer data.

items.title: Serve over HTTPS
items.text:
Jocasta serves only plain HTTP. Put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of it.

By default, the session cookie works only over HTTPS. So to sign in over plain HTTP from an address other than localhost, set server.auth.cookie_secure: false. When the proxy works, remove this setting.

items.title: Caddy
items.text:
Caddy gets and renews the certificate. On the same machine:

jocasta.example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8080
}

If only your network resolves the name, add tls internal. Caddy then signs the certificate itself. Each browser must trust it once.

items.title: Other proxies
items.text: Pass the Host header through without a change. Jocasta compares it with Origin. This lets Jocasta refuse cross-site form posts from browsers that do not send Sec-Fetch-Site. In nginx, use proxy_set_header Host $host;.

items.title: Name the proxy
items.text:
Jocasta limits sign-in attempts for each client address. Behind a proxy, every request comes from the address of the proxy. So all clients share one limit. To prevent this, tell Jocasta to read the client address from X-Forwarded-For:

server:
  trusted_proxies:
    - "127.0.0.1"

List the address or range of each proxy. Caddy, nginx and Traefik set the header.

items.title: Close the plain port
items.text:
If the proxy is on the same machine, listen only on loopback:

server:
  host: "127.0.0.1"

The container image sets JOCASTA_SERVER__HOST=0.0.0.0, and this value wins over the file. So in a container, pass -e JOCASTA_SERVER__HOST=127.0.0.1 to docker run instead.

items.title: Fix common problems
items.text: If your problem is not on this page, ask in GitHub issues. Include the log lines around the problem.

items.title: Devices have no hardware address or vendor
items.text:
On a bridge network, the container reads its own neighbour table. This table contains none of your devices. Use --network host.

For devices on other segments, add a router plugin.

items.title: One phone shows up as several devices
items.text: The phone makes up a new hardware address from time to time. Each address is a new device. Jocasta deletes the devices that you did not edit after 90 days. On your own phone, turn off the private address for your home Wi-Fi.

items.title: A device is missing
items.text: The sweep finds only devices that answer ping. By default, Windows does not answer ping. A router plugin finds such devices in the tables of the router.

items.title: "no usable ICMP socket"
items.text:
If you run the binary without root, its group must be allowed to use unprivileged ICMP. To see the allowed groups, run:

sysctl net.ipv4.ping_group_range

Make the range include the group of Jocasta, or use the container image.

items.title: No mDNS, DNS-SD or SSDP names
items.text: These lookups reach only the segment of Jocasta. DNS-SD and SSDP also need multicast. Use --network host. See How names are chosen.

items.title: The sign-in page keeps coming back
items.text: By default, the session cookie works only over HTTPS. See Serve over HTTPS.

items.title: A form shows "Cross-origin request refused"
items.text: Your reverse proxy changes the Host header. See Serve over HTTPS.

items.title: A plugin reads as "source rejected credentials"
items.text:
Test the plugin alone: jocasta plugin run gateway.

  • RouterOS: the user needs read access. The www-ssl service must be on. Or the www service must be on, with ssl: false.
  • OpenWrt: the login needs the ACL file.
  • Technitium: the user of the token needs View on Logs.
  • An environment variable wins over the file. Check both.

items.title: The Traffic page stays empty
items.text:
• exporters must list the address that the exports come from. If it does not, the log shows the warning "dropping datagrams from a sender not listed in exporters", with that address.
  • On a bridge network, publish the port as UDP: -p 2055:2055/udp.
  • Open the listen port in the firewall of the host.

items.title: Every DNS lookup is counted against the router
items.text: The router forwards the lookups of its clients. In the DHCP settings of the router, give out the address of the resolver. See Record what devices look up.

items.title: Times are hours off
items.text: The container runs in UTC. Set location.timezone, such as Australia/Sydney.

items.title: A notification did not arrive
items.text: In the account menu, the Notifications page shows the last error under the destination. To try again, select Send test. Jocasta does not send a failed message again.

items.title: An MCP client gets a 404
items.text: Set server.mcp.enabled: true, then restart Jocasta.

items.title: Upgrade notes
items.text: What to change or expect when moving to a release, newest first. Read every section after the release you run, and back up first. A release not listed here needs only the usual steps.

items.title: Breaking changes
items.text:
• config: Group retention, location, server settings (#205)

    a config that sets inventory.retention, auth.* or mcp.enabled, or the matching JOCASTA_ variables, now has those settings ignored. Move them to the new paths.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Role Can Viewer Read the inventory. Create read tokens. Editor Also edit devices. Create read/write tokens. Admin Also add users and set what each notification destination gets.

The account that you create on the first run is the only admin.

items.title: Add a user
items.text:
1. Open the account menu, top right, and select Users.
  2. Select Add user.
  3. Enter a username (3 to 100 characters), a first password (8 or more), and a role.
  4. Select Create user.
  5. Give the password to the person.

The web UI cannot yet change a password or role, remove an account, or reset a forgotten password.

items.title: Sessions
items.text:
A sign-in lasts up to 7 days, or 24 hours without use. If you do not tick Remember me, it also ends when the browser closes. To change the limits, set server.auth.session_lifetime and server.auth.idle_timeout.

After 10 wrong passwords, an account gets one try each minute.

items.title: Two-factor authentication
items.text:
1. Open the account menu and select Security.
  2. Select Turn on two-factor authentication.
  3. Scan the QR code with an authenticator app.
  4. Enter the 6-digit code from the app.
  5. Select Turn on.
  6. Save the 10 recovery codes. Jocasta shows them only once. Each code signs you in once without the app.

On the same page, you can make new recovery codes or turn two-factor off. Both actions ask for your password.

items.title: API tokens
items.text:
Scripts and agents use a token to reach the JSON API and the MCP server.

  1. Open the account menu and select API tokens.
  2. Select Create a token.
  3. Enter a name.
  4. Select Viewer (read) or Editor (read_write).
  5. Select an expiry. By default, a token never expires.
  6. Select Create token.
  7. Copy the token. Jocasta shows it only once.

A token cannot do more than its account. When you revoke a token, it stops working immediately.

items.title: Plugins
items.text:
Plugins read what a sweep cannot reach:

  • A router gives the devices on every segment, and what is connected where.
  • A flow export gives who talks to whom.
  • A DNS resolver gives what devices look up.
Plugin Devices and networks Topology Traffic DNS lookups MikroTik RouterOS Yes Yes Through NetFlow OpenWrt Yes Yes Through NetFlow NetFlow Yes Technitium Yes Pi-hole Yes AdGuard Home Yes

items.title: Configure a plugin
items.text:
Each plugin is a block under plugins. The first key is the plugin kind. The second key is an instance name that you choose:

plugins:
  routeros:
    gateway:                 # instance name, shown as the source
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      # ...

The instance name is the source of the facts that the plugin records. Routers and DNS resolvers share one set of names. For example, a routeros instance and a technitium instance cannot both be gateway. A netflow listener can have the same name as its router.

Put passwords in the environment, such as JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD. See Configure. The configuration reference lists every setting.

A source with ssl: false sends its password as plain text. Jocasta shows a warning when it starts.

items.title: Check a plugin
items.text:
jocasta plugin run gateway

This command reads the source once and prints what the source reports. It changes nothing. See CLI.

items.title: Topology
items.text: The Topology page comes from a MikroTik or OpenWrt router. To see the port of each device, also read the switches and access points. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: DNS resolvers
items.text: Technitium, Pi-hole and AdGuard Home give the lookups of each device. See Record what devices look up.

items.title: AdGuard Home
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of an AdGuard Home over its API. Record what devices look up tells what Jocasta records. It also tells how to make each device ask AdGuard Home directly.

plugins:
  adguard:
    resolver:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.53"
      port: 443
      ssl: true
      user: "jocasta"
      password: "change-me"

Put the web interface login in user and password. You can also put the password in JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ADGUARD__RESOLVER__PASSWORD. AdGuard Home has no read-only users, so the login can also change settings. If the server has no login, leave user empty.

In the settings of AdGuard Home, keep the query log on. Keep client address anonymisation off. An anonymised address names no device, so Jocasta counts its lookups against no device.

Each read takes at most 20,000 lookups. If more lookups collect while Jocasta is stopped, it keeps the newest. It logs that it skipped the rest.

items.title: All settings
items.text: The configuration reference lists every plugins.adguard setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: Record what devices look up
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of Technitium, Pi-hole v6 or AdGuard Home. For each device, it keeps hourly counts of each name that the device looked up, blocked or not. If traffic collection is on, the traffic of a device names each address after the names that the device looked up.

Technitium Pi-hole AdGuard Home Answer addresses, to name traffic Yes No Yes Read-only login Yes No No

Jocasta reads each resolver every minute, up to 20,000 lookups each time. It keeps the counts for retention.dns, which is 30 days by default.

items.title: Point devices at the resolver
items.text: Jocasta counts a lookup against the address that asked. If the router forwards the lookups of its clients, Jocasta counts them all against the router. So in the DHCP settings of the router, give out the address of the resolver as the DNS server.

items.title: Check it
items.text:
jocasta plugin run resolver

This command prints the lookups of the last hour, for each device and name.

items.title: NetFlow
items.text:
Jocasta can record which devices talk to each other, and to where on the internet. It reads the flow records that your router exports (NetFlow v5, v9 or IPFIX). It keeps hourly totals for each device for retention.traffic, which is 30 days by default. It does not store single connections.

plugins:
  netflow:
    gateway:
      enabled: true
      listen: ":2055"
      exporters:
        - "192.0.2.1"        # the router's address; anything else is dropped

You must set exporters. Jocasta reads only datagrams from the listed addresses. A device on the same network can forge such an address. So bind listen to an address that only the router reaches. Or, in your firewall, allow the port only from the router.

With host networking, no more setup is necessary. On a bridge network, publish the port as UDP: -p 2055:2055/udp.

items.title: Set up the router
items.text:
Send the flow export of the router to the Jocasta host and port:

  • MikroTik RouterOS: Traffic Flow, as IPFIX.
  • OpenWrt: softflowd, as NetFlow v9.

Export from one router only. If two routers see the same conversation, both report it, and Jocasta counts it twice.

Jocasta shows an internet address by the organisation that announces it. It puts the address on the map by the country where it is registered. For this, it uses IP to ASN data and IP to Country data by DB-IP, licensed under CC BY 4.0.

The world map draws a line from the country of the network to each country that it talked to. Jocasta finds the country of the network from the outside address of the router. This address is private if the ISP puts the router behind carrier-grade NAT. In that case, set the country yourself, by its two-letter code. Jocasta then uses this country, whatever the outside address is:

location:
  country: "AU"

Jocasta uses only the country, to start the lines from its middle. It does not ask for or store a more exact location.

items.title: All settings
items.text: The configuration reference lists every plugins.netflow setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: OpenWrt
items.text:
Jocasta reads OpenWrt over ubus, at http://<router>/ubus. ubus is the JSON-RPC endpoint that LuCI uses. Every router with LuCI serves it, so you do not need to install anything. Jocasta reads the neighbour table, the DHCP leases, the static leases, and the interfaces with their VLANs. For the Topology page, it also reads the ports, the bridge table and the Wi-Fi clients. It changes nothing on the router.

Give Jocasta its own login, which can only read. On the router:

  1. Copy openwrt/jocasta.json to /usr/share/rpcd/acl.d/jocasta.json. This file allows the reads that Jocasta makes and nothing else. The groups of LuCI do not allow reads of the bridge table. So without this file, root also cannot read it.
  2. Hash a password for the login:
uhttpd -m 'change-me'
  1. Add the login to /etc/config/rpcd, with the hash from the last step:
config login
 option username 'jocasta'
 option password '$1$...'
 list read 'jocasta'
  1. Reload rpcd:
/etc/init.d/rpcd reload

Then add the router to Jocasta:

plugins:
  openwrt:
    gateway:                 # instance name, shown as the source
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      user: "jocasta"
      password: "change-me"  # or JOCASTA_PLUGINS__OPENWRT__GATEWAY__PASSWORD
      ssl: false             # true once luci-ssl is installed
      insecure: false        # true for uhttpd's self-signed cert

Test the source with jocasta plugin run gateway. If rpcd refuses the login, or the ACL file is missing, Jocasta reports rejected credentials.

A name that you set under Network → DHCP and DNS → Static Leases ranks above the name that a device asks for. A static lease on RouterOS works the same way. Jocasta names a network after its OpenWrt interface, such as lan or iot. An interface on a VLAN device has the VLAN tag.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
Each OpenWrt table adds this to the Topology page:

  • Bridge table of the kernel: the port behind which each hardware address is. Most current routers have a DSA switch. On a DSA switch, each switch port is a separate device, so the table names the port. An older router has a swconfig switch. On a swconfig switch, all switch ports are one device, so the table names only that device. rpcd reads at most 256 entries of the table. If a bridge has more, Jocasta shows the first 256 and logs a warning.
  • bridge-vlan sections of the network configuration: the VLANs on each port.
  • Station list of iwinfo: which devices are Wi-Fi clients, with their network, band, signal and rate in each direction.
  • Device list of LuCI: the link rate of each port.

By default, OpenWrt runs no neighbour discovery. So an OpenWrt source names no neighbours. But if Jocasta also reads an OpenWrt access point, the router finds the access point among the addresses on its ports.

To read the ports of an OpenWrt access point, add it as another instance with topology_only: true. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: Export traffic flows
items.text:
To record who devices talk to, install softflowd and send its exports to the Jocasta host. Then set up the NetFlow listener. In this example, the Jocasta host is 192.0.2.10:

opkg update && opkg install softflowd    # OpenWrt 24.10 and older
apk update && apk add softflowd          # OpenWrt 25.12 and newer
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].enabled='1'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].host_port='192.0.2.10:2055'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].export_version='9'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].track_ipv6='1'
uci set softflowd.@softflowd[0].timeout='maxlife=300'
uci delete softflowd.@softflowd[0].sampling_rate
uci commit softflowd
/etc/init.d/softflowd enable
/etc/init.d/softflowd start

Each line changes a default. With the defaults, Jocasta does not see some of the traffic:

  • export_version 9 carries IPv6. The default, 5, cannot. IPFIX (10) also works.
  • track_ipv6 records IPv6 conversations, not only IPv4.
  • maxlife=300 reports a long download every five minutes. Without it, softflowd reports a conversation only when it ends. So a stream that runs all evening shows in the hour when it stopped.
  • When you delete sampling_rate, softflowd counts every packet. The default, 100, counts one packet in 100. Jocasta scales sampled counts back up. But it can miss a conversation of only a few packets.

softflowd watches br-lan, the default LAN bridge. To record another segment, such as a VLAN on br-lan.20, add a softflowd section for its interface. Give that section its own pid_file and control_socket. In exporters, list the LAN address of the router, because the exports come from that address.

items.title: All settings
items.text: The configuration reference lists every plugins.openwrt setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: Pi-hole
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of a Pi-hole v6 over its API. Record what devices look up tells what Jocasta records. It also tells how to make each device ask Pi-hole directly. Pi-hole does not log answer addresses, so its lookups do not name traffic.

plugins:
  pihole:
    resolver:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.53"
      port: 443
      ssl: true
      insecure: true         # for Pi-hole's self-signed certificate
      password: "change-me"

To prepare the server:

  1. In Pi-hole's web interface, create an app password.
  2. Put it in password, or in JOCASTA_PLUGINS__PIHOLE__RESOLVER__PASSWORD.

Pi-hole has no read-only login, so the app password can also change settings. A new app password signs out every session. This includes the session of Jocasta. Jocasta signs in again on its next read. If the Pi-hole has no password, leave password empty.

Keep the privacy level of Pi-hole at the level that shows everything. A level that hides domains or clients also hides them from Jocasta.

Each read takes at most 20,000 lookups. If more lookups collect while Jocasta is stopped, it keeps the newest. It logs that it skipped the rest.

items.title: All settings
items.text: The configuration reference lists every plugins.pihole setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS
items.text:
Jocasta reads RouterOS over its REST API:

plugins:
  routeros:
    gateway:                 # instance name, shown as the source
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      user: "jocasta"        # a read-only user is enough
      password: "change-me"  # or JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD
      ssl: true
      insecure: true         # RouterOS serves a self-signed cert unless you import one

Before you start the server, test the source with jocasta plugin run gateway. See CLI.

items.title: Topology
items.text:
Each RouterOS table adds this to the Topology page:

  • Bridge host table: the port behind which each hardware address is. If the bridge has VLAN filtering on, it also gives the VLAN.
  • Neighbour discovery (MNDP or LLDP): the name of the switch or access point on each port. By default, RouterOS runs it on the LAN interface list. See /ip neighbor discovery-settings.
  • Wi-Fi registration table: which devices are Wi-Fi clients, with their network, band, signal and rate in each direction. It comes from the wifi package or the wireless package. A router that manages access points with CAPsMAN also lists their clients.
  • Ethernet monitor: the link rate of each Ethernet and SFP port, and the fastest rate that both ends offer.

To read the ports of a MikroTik switch or access point, add it as another instance with topology_only: true. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: Export traffic flows
items.text:
To record who devices talk to, send Traffic Flow to the Jocasta host. Then set up the NetFlow listener. In this example, the Jocasta host is 192.0.2.10:

/ip traffic-flow set enabled=yes interfaces=all
/ip traffic-flow target add dst-address=192.0.2.10 port=2055 version=ipfix

items.title: All settings
items.text: The configuration reference lists every plugins.routeros setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: Technitium
items.text:
Jocasta reads the query log of a Technitium DNS Server over its HTTP API. Record what devices look up tells what Jocasta records. It also tells how to make each device ask the server directly.

plugins:
  technitium:
    resolver:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.53"
      port: 53443
      ssl: true
      insecure: true         # for the server's self-signed certificate
      token: "change-me"

To prepare the server:

  1. In Apps, App Store, install Query Logs (Sqlite). Technitium keeps a query log only through an app like this one.
  2. In Administration, Users, add a user for Jocasta.
  3. In Administration, Permissions, give that user View on the Logs section and nothing else.
  4. Sign in as that user. In the user menu, select Create API Token.
  5. Put the token in token, or in JOCASTA_PLUGINS__TECHNITIUM__RESOLVER__TOKEN.

If more than one app logs queries, set log_app to the app to read. Use the name that the Apps page shows.

In a cluster, each node logs the lookups that it answered to its own disk. Add one entry for each node, at the node's own address. Do not use a virtual address that the nodes share, such as a VRRP address. It reaches only one node at a time, so Jocasta does not read the lookups of the other node. The primary node copies the token and the log app to every node.

items.title: All settings
items.text: The configuration reference lists every plugins.technitium setting, with its default and allowed values.

items.title: Show what is plugged in where
items.text:
The Topology page shows the network from the internet down. It shows the router, switches, access points, and each device on its port or Wi-Fi network. The data comes from the bridge and Wi-Fi tables of each MikroTik and OpenWrt router that Jocasta reads. If a switch or access point announces itself to the router, the page shows it with the devices behind it.

To see the switch port of each device, also read the switch, with topology_only: true:

plugins:
  routeros:
    gateway:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.1"
      # ...
    switch_core:
      enabled: true
      host: "192.0.2.2"
      user: "jocasta"
      password: "change-me"
      topology_only: true    # ports only; the router lists the devices

A topology_only source finds no devices. So its management address cannot change the name of a network. Jocasta reads every RouterOS and OpenWrt source at each scan.devices.interval.

jocasta plugin run switch_core prints the ports of the switch, the addresses on each port, and the neighbours of the switch.

For what the tables of each router add, see RouterOS and OpenWrt. For how to read the page, see Tour the web UI.

items.title: Configuration reference
items.text:
This page lists every setting that Jocasta reads, with its type, default and allowed values. Configure tells how Jocasta reads and overrides settings. jocasta.example.yaml has the same settings, in a file that you can copy.

Each setting can also come from an environment variable. The name is JOCASTA_, then the path of the setting in capitals, with a double underscore between levels. A single underscore stays part of the key. For example, scan.devices.resolve_mdns is JOCASTA_SCAN__DEVICES__RESOLVE_MDNS. For a plugin or notification setting, the instance or destination name is one level of the path. For example, plugins.routeros.gateway.password is JOCASTA_PLUGINS__ROUTEROS__GATEWAY__PASSWORD.

Types:

  • duration: a number and a unit, such as 90s, 15m or 6h. The units are s, m and h. There is no unit for days, so 30 days is 720h.
  • list: a YAML list.
  • map: YAML keys and values.

items.title: server
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description server.host string localhost An address or host name Where the web server listens. 0.0.0.0 listens on every interface. The container image sets 0.0.0.0. server.port int 8080 1 to 65535 The port the web server listens on. server.trusted_proxies list empty Addresses or CIDR prefixes, such as 192.0.2.1 or 10.0.0.0/8 Reverse proxy addresses whose forwarding headers the server trusts to identify the client. Empty reads the client address from the connection directly. server.cors.allowed_origins list empty Origins as scheme://host[:port] Browser origins besides the server's own that may read /api. Empty sends no CORS headers. server.auth.session_lifetime duration 168h A duration The longest a sign-in lasts, whatever the activity. server.auth.idle_timeout duration 24h A duration How long a session survives with no requests. server.auth.cookie_secure bool true true, false Sends the session cookie over HTTPS only. Set false to sign in over plain HTTP from anywhere but localhost. server.mcp.enabled bool false true, false Serves the MCP endpoint at /mcp. While off, /mcp answers 404.

items.title: db
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description db.path string . A directory Where the SQLite file lives. The container image sets /data. db.name string jocasta.db A file name The SQLite file's name.

items.title: logger
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description logger.level string info debug, info, warn, error The lowest level logged. Any other value logs at info. logger.format string json json, text How each log line is written. Any value but text writes JSON.

items.title: inventory
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description inventory.online_window duration 15m A duration How long after its last sighting a device counts as online. Past it, a watched device goes quiet. inventory.address_grace duration 6h A duration How long an address can go unseen before a later sweep that finds the device elsewhere retires it. Raise it on a network with long DHCP leases.

items.title: retention
items.text:
Once an hour, Jocasta deletes the records that are older than their window. 0s keeps that kind of record forever.

Key Type Default Allowed values Description retention.history duration 2160h (90 days) A duration; 0s keeps forever How long Jocasta keeps the change log and the scan log. retention.traffic duration 720h (30 days) A duration; 0s keeps forever How long Jocasta keeps the hourly traffic totals. retention.dns duration 720h (30 days) A duration; 0s keeps forever How long Jocasta keeps the hourly lookup counts, and the addresses in the answers to lookups. retention.devices duration 2160h (90 days) A duration; 0s keeps forever How long Jocasta keeps a device after a scan last saw it. Jocasta keeps a device that you labelled, grouped, typed, noted, ignored or watched.

items.title: location
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description location.country string empty A two-letter country code, such as AU The country from which the world map draws its lines. If empty, Jocasta uses the outside address of the router. This address cannot find the country of a network behind carrier-grade NAT. See NetFlow. location.timezone string empty An IANA zone name, such as Australia/Sydney The zone in which Jocasta shows times. If empty, Jocasta uses TZ or the zone of the system, which is UTC in a container. Jocasta always stores times in UTC.

items.title: networks
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description networks list the host's network Prefixes, such as 192.0.2.0/24 The prefixes that the sweep covers at each interval. Jocasta records each address that it finds under the network that contains it. If the list is empty, Jocasta sweeps the network of the host's default route. It does this only if the network is a /22 or smaller.

items.title: scan
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description scan.source string sweep:<hostname> Any name The source name of the sweeps that run at each interval. Set it in a container, where the host name changes on every run. A new name starts a new source. Past scans stay under the old name. scan.devices.enabled bool true true, false Sweeps networks on a timer. scan.devices.interval duration 5m A duration How often the sweep runs. scan.devices.rate int 1000 A whole number The most ICMP probes sent per second. scan.devices.rounds int 2 A whole number The number of probes to each address before Jocasta counts the address as down. scan.devices.wait duration 2s A duration How long to wait for replies after the last probe. scan.devices.resolve_names bool true true, false Looks up reverse DNS for each address that answered. See Name devices. scan.devices.resolve_macs bool true true, false Reads the neighbour table for hardware addresses. scan.devices.resolve_mdns bool true true, false Asks each device without a reverse DNS name for its name over mDNS. scan.devices.resolve_netbios bool true true, false Asks each device still without a name over NetBIOS. scan.devices.resolve_dnssd bool true true, false Asks for the services that devices advertise. Names each device that still has no name after the name that it gives its services. Needs host networking. scan.devices.resolve_ssdp bool true true, false Searches over SSDP. Names each device that still has no name after its UPnP friendlyName. Needs host networking. scan.ports.enabled bool false true, false Probes every known address for open TCP ports on a timer. scan.ports.interval duration 6h A duration How often the port scan runs. scan.ports.custom string empty Ports and ranges, such as 22,80,443,8000-8100; 1-65535 for every port The ports to probe. If empty, Jocasta uses a preset. Jocasta also probes each address on the ports that its device advertises. scan.ports.concurrency int 64 A whole number The most connections a scan opens at once. Lower it on a router with a small connection table.

items.title: plugins
items.text: By default, plugins are off. Each instance is under its kind, with a name that you choose as its key. An instance is off, unless it has enabled: true. See Plugins.

items.title: plugins.routeros
items.text:
A MikroTik RouterOS router, switch or access point.

Key Type Default Allowed values Description plugins.routeros.<instance>.enabled bool false true, false Reads this source. plugins.routeros.<instance>.host string none, required An address or host name, without a port Where the REST API is. plugins.routeros.<instance>.port int 80, or 443 with ssl 1 to 65535 The REST API's port. plugins.routeros.<instance>.user string empty A RouterOS user A read-only user is enough. plugins.routeros.<instance>.password string empty Any The user's password. plugins.routeros.<instance>.ssl bool false true, false Uses HTTPS. Without it, the password goes over the network as plain text, and Jocasta logs a warning. plugins.routeros.<instance>.insecure bool false true, false Skips certificate checks, for RouterOS's self-signed certificate. plugins.routeros.<instance>.timeout duration 10s A duration The longest one read may take. plugins.routeros.<instance>.topology_only bool false true, false Reads only what is connected to this switch or access point. The router lists its devices. See Show what is plugged in where.

items.title: plugins.netflow
items.text:
A NetFlow listener for a router's flow exports.

Key Type Default Allowed values Description plugins.netflow.<instance>.enabled bool false true, false Runs this listener. plugins.netflow.<instance>.listen string :2055 A UDP address, such as :2055 or 192.0.2.10:2055 Where the listener binds. plugins.netflow.<instance>.exporters list none, required IP addresses The routers that can send. Jocasta discards datagrams from all other addresses.

items.title: plugins.technitium
items.text:
A Technitium DNS Server node.

Key Type Default Allowed values Description plugins.technitium.<instance>.enabled bool false true, false Reads this server's query log. plugins.technitium.<instance>.host string none, required An address or host name, without a port The address of this node. Do not use a virtual address that the nodes share. It reaches only one node at a time. plugins.technitium.<instance>.port int 5380, or 53443 with ssl 1 to 65535 The web service's port. plugins.technitium.<instance>.token string empty An API token A token for a user granted Logs: View. plugins.technitium.<instance>.ssl bool false true, false Uses HTTPS. Without it, the token goes over the network as plain text, and Jocasta logs a warning. plugins.technitium.<instance>.insecure bool false true, false Skips certificate checks, for a self-signed certificate. plugins.technitium.<instance>.log_app string empty An app name, as the Apps page lists it The app whose log Jocasta reads. Necessary only if more than one installed app logs queries. plugins.technitium.<instance>.timeout duration 10s A duration The longest one read may take.

items.title: notify
items.text:
Each destination is under notify, with a name that you choose as its key. It has exactly one service block: ntfy, webhook or http. To select the changes that a destination gets, use the Notifications page in the account menu. See Notifications.

Key Type Default Allowed values Description notify.<name>.enabled bool true true, false Sends to this destination. A destination is on unless it says false. notify.<name>.timeout duration 10s A duration The longest one send may take.

items.title: ntfy
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description notify.<name>.ntfy.url string none, required The topic's URL, as ntfy shows it Where Jocasta publishes messages, such as https://ntfy.example.com/jocasta. notify.<name>.ntfy.token string empty An ntfy access token For a server that requires one. notify.<name>.ntfy.priority int 0 0 to 5 ntfy's priority, from 1 (min) to 5 (max). 0 leaves it to the server.

items.title: webhook
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description notify.<name>.webhook.url string none, required An HTTP or HTTPS URL Where the signed JSON POST goes. notify.<name>.webhook.secret string none, required Any Keys the signature on each request. See Check a webhook's signature.

items.title: http
items.text: Key Type Default Allowed values Description notify.<name>.http.url string none, required An HTTP or HTTPS URL Where the request goes. It can contain the token of the service. Jocasta never logs or shows it. notify.<name>.http.headers map empty Header names and values Sent with every request, such as Authorization. A Content-Type here replaces application/json. notify.<name>.http.body string none, required A Go template The request body. See Send to another service for recipes.
